name: Dusty mahogany
lede: Dusty mahogany is a muted reddish brown built the plain way, by putting the modifier "dusty" in front of [[mahogany]], the reddish-brown timber color.

sections.title: A modifier on mahogany
sections.body:
"Dusty" here is a grammar move, not a dye or a place: it softens [[mahogany]] toward grey the way "dusty rose" softens rose [1]. Our color library files it as a modifier compound rather than a named historical color [1].

The same hex also sits near a Japanese traditional name in our data, Kōrozen (黄櫨染, "sumac-dyed"), listed among the traditional colors of Japan, but the library gives no date for when that name was first recorded, so it stays undocumented here [2]. The nearest named color in our graph is [[chestnut-leather-brown]], at a color distance (ΔE2000) of 2.6, essentially the same shade; [[mahogany]] itself sits 4.6 away and reads more vivid by comparison [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this brown in 2,420 of 23,781 paintings, about 10.2 percent, one of the more common colors in this group, as photographed [4]. It peaks in the 1560s (38 of 159 paintings from that decade), with Pontormo's portraits showing it in well over half their canvases, and Juan de Juanes and Bronzino close behind [4]. The earliest dated match is a carved wooden beam fragment from the year 550, a floor set by what survives and was photographed, not a first appearance, and long before the Japanese name on record for the same hue [4]. These are museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a computed color comparison, not a pigment identification [4].
